s:
Consider the following statements regarding the applicability of Fundamental Rights:
1. Articles 23 and 24 are denied to all foreigners.
2. Enemy aliens do not enjoy the safeguards under Article 22 in the circumstances specified in Article 22(3).
3. Companies can claim rights available to all persons, but cannot claim the rights under Article 19.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statement 1 is false because Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens from specified safeguards, and companies may claim all-persons rights but not Article 19 rights.
tq: Find the swapped pair: Articles 23 and 24 are not among the rights denied to aliens.
sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

s: A foreign national ordinarily residing in India seeks protection against discrimination based solely on place of birth under Article 15. Which of the following is the most appropriate constitutional position?
o: The protection is available because Article 15 is available to every person.
The protection under Article 15 is available only to citizens.
The protection is available only if the person is an enemy alien.
The protection is available only through Article 23.
x: Article 15 is among the Fundamental Rights available only to citizens. It is not an all-persons right available to foreign nationals merely because they reside in India.
tq: Apply the citizen-only list to a short factual situation rather than recalling the list mechanically.
sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

s: Which one of the following Articles is available to both citizens and foreigners, subject to constitutional exceptions?
x: Article 21 is available to all persons. Articles 19, 16 and 29 are included among the rights available only to citizens.
tq: Discriminate between the closely placed citizen-only Articles 16, 19 and 29 and the all-persons Article 21.
sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 15
b. Article 20
c. Article 29
d. Article 27

List-II (Availability)
i. Only citizens
ii. All persons
iii. Only citizens
iv. All persons

option codes:
x: Articles 15 and 29 are available only to citizens, while Articles 20 and 27 are available to all persons. Therefore, the matching is a–i, b–ii, c–iii and d–iv.
tq: Start from the sure pairs: Article 15 is citizen-only and Article 20 is an all-persons right.
sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 23 — Right to freedom of religion
Article 14 — Equality before law and equal protection of laws
x: Article 23 deals with the right against exploitation, including prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour. The right to freedom of religion is covered by Articles 25 to 28.
tq: Find the wrong group–article association by checking the standard six-group classification.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: Part III of the Constitution of India extends from:
x: Part III contains Fundamental Rights and extends from Article 12 to Article 35.
tq: Test the exact constitutional range directly, with neighbouring Parts as plausible distractors.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s:
Arrange the following groups of Fundamental Rights in the order in which their article ranges occur in Part III, beginning with the earliest:
A. Right against exploitation
B. Right to equality
C. Cultural and educational rights
D. Right to freedom of religion
x: The sequence is right to equality (Articles 14–18), right against exploitation (23–24), right to freedom of religion (25–28), and cultural and educational rights (29–30).
tq: Use the first and last article ranges to place the groups in sequence.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: Which one of the following correctly represents the present number and original number of groups of Fundamental Rights?
x: The Constitution originally contained seven groups of Fundamental Rights. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment, leaving six groups at present.
tq: Separate the original and present figures before examining the options.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 and is presently protected as a legal or constitutional right under:
x: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed Article 31 from the Fundamental Rights chapter. Property is now protected under Article 300A in Part XII as a constitutional/legal right.
tq: Use the amendment–article–Part chain instead of confusing the former Article 31 with the present provision.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right expressly included in Part III?
o: Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years
x: The right to employment is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
tq: Distinguish claimed socio-economic rights from rights expressly placed in Part III.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Equal pay for equal work — Article 39(d)
2. Right to vote — Article 326 and election laws
3. Right to shelter — Express Fundamental Right in Part III
4. Right to property — Article 300A
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d), voting is a statutory right connected with Article 326 and election laws, and property is protected under Article 300A. Right to shelter is not an express Fundamental Right, though courts have read it into Article 21.
tq: Check whether each claimed right is express, derivative, statutory or a Directive Principle.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: The right to education for children between six and fourteen years is a Fundamental Right under:
o: Article 30, inserted by the 73rd Amendment Act
Article 19, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act
Article 24, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002
x: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, making education for children aged six to fourteen a Fundamental Right. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 gives effect to it.
tq: Link the age range, Article 21A and the 86th Amendment without confusing them with child-labour provisions.
sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

s: Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
o: They can be enforced only after Parliament passes a law under Article 35.
They are enforceable only by the High Courts.
They are non-justiciable because they are political principles.
An aggrieved person may directly approach the Supreme Court under Article 32.
x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, and Article 32 permits an aggrieved person to move the Supreme Court directly for their enforcement. High Courts can also enforce them under Article 226, along with other legal rights.
tq: Identify the constitutional remedy that directly establishes justiciability: Article 32.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamental Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions where the Constitution permits such restrictions.
2. Courts examine the reasonableness of restrictions through judicial review.
3. Every Fundamental Right is absolute and cannot be regulated by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Fundamental Rights are qualified rather than absolute, and courts review restrictions for constitutional validity and reasonableness. Statement 3 is false.
tq: Reject the absolute claim and retain the two statements describing the restriction-and-review framework.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: How many grounds of reasonable restriction are listed in Article 19 in all?
x: Article 19 contains eleven grounds of reasonable restriction in all. These restrictions must be imposed by law and must fall within constitutionally recognised grounds.
tq: Test the precise numerical detail with nearby figures as distractors.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Which one of the following is a negative right, in the sense that it primarily limits State action?
x: Article 20 is a negative right that limits State action in relation to conviction for offences. Articles 21A, 29 and 30 are examples of positive rights conferring particular privileges or protections.
tq: Distinguish negative restraints on the State from positive rights that confer privileges.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Which one of the following sets consists only of examples of positive Fundamental Rights?
x: Articles 21A, 29 and 30 confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights. The other sets contain negative rights that primarily restrict State action.
tq: Classify each option by the direction of the right rather than by its subject title.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Which one of the following Articles is NOT included among the provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power?
x: Articles 15, 17, 18, 20 and 24 are identified as provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power. Article 19 permits reasonable restrictions on specified grounds and is therefore not in that group.
tq: Find the exception within a closely related Article list.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Fundamental Rights are primarily enforceable against the State, but which of the following Articles also operate against private persons in the situations covered by them?
x: Although most Fundamental Rights operate against State action, Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 also impose obligations relevant to private persons. The other combinations do not represent the specified group.
tq: Use the exception-to-the-general-rule method: identify the Articles that can bind private persons.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: The model for the Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was principally drawn from the:
x: The Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was modelled principally on the United States Bill of Rights.
tq: Test the foreign constitutional source directly, using other constitutional models as distractors.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Which one of the following correctly describes Fundamental Rights?
o: They are both natural and legal rights and protect individuals as well as minorities.
They are only legal rights and have no natural-rights character.
They protect only minorities and not individuals.
They are exclusively political rights available only during elections.
x: Fundamental Rights have both natural and legal dimensions and are intended to protect individuals and minorities. They are not confined to electoral or exclusively political rights.
tq: Choose the comprehensive description and reject options that use exclusive language.
sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

s: Which authority alone is empowered under Article 33 to restrict the application of Fundamental Rights to members of the armed forces and specified security services?
o: The Supreme Court by judicial order
x: Article 33 empowers Parliament alone to restrict or abrogate the application of Fundamental Rights for members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence organisations and related staff, including specified non-combatants.
tq: Ask who would do this job: Article 33 expressly assigns the power to Parliament, not the executive or States.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 33:
1. Parliament may restrict Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces.
2. The power may extend to specified non-combatant employees such as cooks and barbers.
3. State Legislatures may exercise the same power independently for maintaining public order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 33 gives the power exclusively to Parliament, so Statement 3 is false.
tq: Spot the wrong authority in Statement 3 while retaining the specific scope of Article 33.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 34 is correct?
o: It automatically suspends Articles 20 and 21 whenever martial law is declared.
It deals with preventive detention during a National Emergency only.
It empowers State Legislatures to declare martial law throughout India.
It permits restriction of Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and allows Parliament to indemnify officials; martial law is not defined in the Constitution.
x: Article 34 concerns restrictions on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and permits Parliament to indemnify officials for acts connected with it. The Constitution does not define martial law.
tq: Combine the Article 34 subject, Parliament’s indemnity power and the constitutional omission on definition.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: Under Article 35, which body has exclusive legislative competence to make laws on the matters specified in that Article?
x: Article 35 assigns legislative power exclusively to Parliament for matters including Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and for prescribing punishments for offences under Part III. The purpose is uniformity throughout India.
tq: Apply the exclusive-authority trap to distinguish Parliament from State Legislatures.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 33
b. Article 34
c. Article 35
d. Article 359

List-II (Provision)
i. Restriction during martial law and indemnity by Parliament
ii. President’s order suspending enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights
iii. Parliament’s exclusive power to legislate on specified Part III matters
iv. Restriction of Fundamental Rights of specified forces and security services

option codes:
x: Article 33 concerns specified forces and security services, Article 34 concerns martial law, Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive legislative power on specified matters, and Article 359 concerns the President’s order suspending enforcement of named rights.
tq: Start with the distinctive pairs Article 33–forces and Article 34–martial law, then complete the remaining matches.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 358 and 359?
o: Article 358 operates only during armed rebellion, whereas Article 359 operates only during financial emergency.
Article 358 concerns automatic suspension of Article 19 during war or external aggression, whereas Article 359 concerns a Presidential order suspending enforcement of named Fundamental Rights.
Article 358 is a power of the Supreme Court, whereas Article 359 is a power of Parliament.
Article 358 suspends enforcement of all Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 359 suspends only Article 19.
x: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 only when the Emergency is based on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. Article 359 enables the President to suspend enforcement of named Fundamental Rights by order, but not Articles 20 and 21.
tq: Split the two similar provisions by authority, trigger and scope instead of treating both as identical emergency powers.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: A constitutional amendment affecting a Fundamental Right is challenged before the Supreme Court. Which of the following principles is applicable?
o: Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights only through a constitutional amendment, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights through an ordinary statute without limitation.
Only State Legislatures may amend Fundamental Rights.
x: Fundamental Rights may be altered through the constitutional amendment procedure, but the amendment is subject to the basic-structure doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). An ordinary law cannot amend the Constitution.
tq: Distinguish constitutional amendment from ordinary legislation and apply the basic-structure limitation.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: The basic-structure limitation on Parliament’s amending power is associated with which case and year?
x: The basic-structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973. It limits Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution, including provisions relating to Fundamental Rights.
tq: Link the doctrine with its leading case and year, while avoiding nearby constitutional cases.
sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

s: Which doctrine states that a law is void only to the extent of its inconsistency with Fundamental Rights, while the separable valid portion continues to operate?
x: The doctrine of severability invalidates only the inconsistent portion of a law, provided that portion can be separated from the valid remainder.
tq: Use the exact meaning of the doctrine rather than the associated case.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: The doctrine of Eclipse primarily applies to a law which is:
o: A pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
A post-Constitution law violating the rights of non-citizens only
A constitutional amendment violating the basic structure
A contractual provision waived by a citizen
x: The doctrine of eclipse mainly applies to pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights. Such laws become dormant rather than completely dead.
tq: Discriminate between the scope of Eclipse and the other doctrines.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s:
Consider the following statements about the doctrine of Eclipse:
1. An inconsistent pre-Constitution law becomes dormant rather than being completely wiped out.
2. The law may revive when the constitutional conflict is removed.
3. The doctrine was applied in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements are correct. In Bhikaji Narain Dhakras, the inconsistent law was treated as eclipsed and capable of revival after removal of the conflict through the First Amendment.
tq: Test the meaning, consequence and leading case together.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: Which case is associated with the application of the doctrine of Waiver in relation to Fundamental Rights?
o: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
Motor General Traders v. State of AP
x: In Basheshar Nath v. CIT (1959), it was held that a person cannot waive a Fundamental Right.
tq: Match the doctrine with its leading case.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: With reference to the doctrine of Waiver, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: A person cannot waive a Fundamental Right, though statutory or contractual rights may be given up.
Only constitutional rights may be voluntarily given up.
Waiver applies only to rights available to non-citizens.
A citizen may permanently waive any Fundamental Right by contract.
x: Fundamental Rights cannot be waived by an individual. Statutory and contractual rights, unlike Fundamental Rights, may be relinquished.
tq: Apply the distinction between Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Doctrine)
(a) Eclipse
(b) Severability
(c) Waiver
(d) Prospective overruling

List-II (Meaning)
(i) Ruling operates only for the future
(ii) A person cannot give up a Fundamental Right
(iii) Inconsistent law remains dormant and may revive
(iv) Only the inconsistent portion of a law is void

Select the correct answer using the code given below:
x: Eclipse means dormancy and possible revival; Severability preserves the separable valid part; Waiver cannot operate against Fundamental Rights; Prospective overruling operates only in the future.
tq: Start from the sure pair and eliminate codes.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Severability — State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills
x: State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is associated with the extension of the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws affecting non-citizens. Severability is associated with cases such as A.K. Gopalan, R.M.D.C. and Motor General Traders.
tq: Find the wrongly assigned case rather than recalling the doctrine alone.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: The decision in State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills is significant because it:
o: Introduced the doctrine of prospective overruling
Applied Eclipse to a post-Constitution law in relation to non-citizens
Established that a person may waive Fundamental Rights
Held that Fundamental Rights can never be amended
x: Ambica Mills (1974) extended the doctrine of Eclipse to post-Constitution laws operating against non-citizens.
tq: Use the distinctive qualification attached to a famous case.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: The doctrine of Progressive Interpretation treats the Constitution as:
o: A rigid document confined to the original understanding of its framers
A document subordinate to ordinary legislation
A document applicable only to disputes involving citizens
A living document to be read in accordance with present needs
x: Progressive Interpretation reads the Constitution as a living document capable of responding to present social and constitutional needs.
tq: Identify the central idea of the doctrine from its constitutional application.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: Which case is associated with the widening of Article 21 through progressive interpretation?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened the interpretation of Article 21 and is an important example of progressive constitutional interpretation.
tq: Link the interpretive doctrine with its constitutional example.
sec: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

s: Payment of wages below the minimum wage to labourers, in the circumstances recognised by the Supreme Court, amounts to:
o: A restriction on freedom of association under Article 19(4)
x: Payment below the minimum wage may amount to forced labour under Article 23, as recognised in the PUDR/Asiad case of 1982.
tq: Translate a factual situation into the applicable Fundamental Right.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s: A person employing a child below fourteen years in a factory or mine would violate:
x: Article 24 prohibits the employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment.
tq: Separate the child-exploitation provision from forced labour and discrimination provisions.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s: Denial of admission to a State-aided educational institution solely on the ground of religion, race, caste or language is prohibited by:
x: Article 29(2) prohibits denial of admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on these grounds.
tq: Identify the specific clause governing admission to State-aided institutions.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Excluding Dalits from a public well may violate Article 15(2).
2. Excluding Dalits from a public shop may violate Article 17.
3. The protections under Articles 15(2) and 17 may operate against private persons in such situations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Exclusion of Dalits from public facilities can attract Articles 15(2) and 17, and these protections are not confined to State action in such cases.
tq: Combine the prohibited conduct, constitutional provisions and horizontal application.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s: A prohibition imposed on an association can be treated as a restriction under Article 19(4) only when it is based on:
o: The grounds constitutionally permitted under Article 19(4)
Any reason considered desirable by the executive
An ordinance that is immune from judicial review
x: Restrictions on freedom of association under Article 19(4) must be based on the constitutionally specified grounds and remain subject to constitutional scrutiny.
tq: Ask whether the restriction fits the constitutional grounds rather than accepting executive discretion.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s: A violation of Articles 19 or 21 by a purely private individual ordinarily gives rise to:
o: An ordinary legal remedy rather than a writ remedy against the private individual
A remedy exclusively before the Election Commission
An automatic writ petition under Article 32 against that individual
x: Where the alleged violation is by a private individual and does not involve enforceable public-law action, the ordinary legal remedy is generally available rather than a writ.
tq: Distinguish enforceable public-law rights from an ordinary private-law remedy.
sec: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

s: Under Article 13(1), laws in force before the commencement of the Constitution which are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are:
o: Void only to the extent of inconsistency
Valid even to the extent of inconsistency
Void in their entirety in every case
x: Article 13(1) renders a pre-Constitution law void only to the extent that it conflicts with Fundamental Rights. It does not refer to laws existing before Independence as such.
tq: Watch the precise constitutional time reference and the words ‘to the extent’.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court
Only an Act passed by Parliament
x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making a law which:
o: Changes the distribution of legislative powers only
Regulates contractual rights between private parties alone
Creates a new district within a State
Abridges or takes away the rights conferred by Part III
x: Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III; such a law is void to that extent.
tq: Match the constitutional clause with the prohibited legislative action.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s: Which constitutional amendment inserted Article 13(4), excluding constitutional amendments made under Article 368 from the operation of Article 13?
x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment Act, 1971 inserted Article 13(4), providing that Article 13 would not apply to constitutional amendments made under Article 368.
tq: Pair the specific clause with the correct amendment year.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s:
Consider the following statements regarding constitutional amendments and Article 13:
1. In Shankari Prasad, the Supreme Court held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights.
2. In Golaknath, Fundamental Rights were given a transcendental position and Parliament was held unable to abridge them.
3. Kesavananda Bharati held that Fundamental Rights could be amended subject to the basic structure limitation.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements correctly describe the holdings associated with Shankari Prasad, Golaknath and Kesavananda Bharati.
tq: Track the constitutional position across successive landmark decisions.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional significance of Article 13?
o: It prevents courts from examining delegated legislation.
It applies only to laws enacted before the Constitution.
It makes Fundamental Rights subordinate to ordinary legislation.
It provides the basis for judicial review and gives Fundamental Rights precedence over ordinary law.
x: Article 13 is the constitutional basis of judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over ordinary law.
tq: Choose the option capturing both the function and effect of Article 13.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s:
Arrange the following decisions and amendments in chronological order:
A. Kesavananda Bharati case
B. Shankari Prasad case
C. Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment
D. Golaknath case
x: The correct order is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), Twenty-fourth Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
tq: Fix the earliest and latest events first, then place the middle developments.
sec: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which constitutional provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
x: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
tq: Associate the famous description with the exact Article, not merely with Part III generally.
sec: Descriptions of Fundamental Rights - who said

s:
Which of the following is included within the expression ‘State’ under Article 12 of the Constitution of India?
1. The Government and Parliament of India
2. The Government and Legislature of each State
3. All local authorities
4. Other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Article 12 includes the Union Government and Parliament, State Governments and Legislatures, local authorities, and other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India.
tq: Use complete constitutional enumeration and check whether any category has been omitted.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: Which one of the following cases laid down the tests for determining whether a body is an instrumentality or agency of the State?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
x: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979) laid down the tests for identifying an instrumentality or agency of the State.
tq: Match the case with its distinctive constitutional holding rather than its year alone.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib:
1. A society running a Regional Engineering College was treated as ‘State’.
2. The constitutional test depends on how the body was created and controlled, not merely on its legal form.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: In Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981), the society running a Regional Engineering College was held to be ‘State’. The Court emphasised creation and control rather than the formal legal form of the body.
tq: Separate the substance of governmental control from the formal label of an institution.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: In which of the following cases was it held that a body may be regarded as ‘State’ when it is financially, functionally and administratively dominated by the Government?
o: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
x: Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) held that financial, functional and administrative domination by the Government is a significant basis for treating a body as ‘State’.
tq: Use the three-part domination test as the identifying phrase for the correct case.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: Which one of the following was the principal holding in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967)?
o: Private bodies are always subject to writ jurisdiction
A society running a Regional Engineering College is not a public authority
Only bodies incorporated directly by Parliament can be ‘State’
Statutory bodies are included within ‘other authorities’
x: Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967) recognised statutory bodies as ‘other authorities’ for the purposes of Article 12.
tq: Distinguish the statutory-body principle from the later instrumentality tests.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. A body’s formal legal form is by itself decisive in determining whether it is ‘State’ under Article 12.
2. Government share capital may be relevant in applying instrumentality or agency tests.
3. Deep and pervasive governmental control may be relevant in determining whether a body is ‘State’.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 2 and 3 are correct because government share capital and deep and pervasive control are relevant factors. Statement 1 is false because Ajay Hasia held that creation and control, rather than form alone, are material.
tq: Spot the absolute formulation that wrongly makes legal form conclusive.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: Which of the following is NOT ordinarily correct regarding writ petitions against private bodies?
o: The ordinary rule is subject to the circumstance of State collusion
Writs ordinarily lie against every private body because Article 12 includes all institutions
A writ may become maintainable where the State acts in collusion with a private body
Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies
x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely because they perform an activity. An exception may arise where the State acts in collusion with the private body.
tq: Reject the option that uses an overbroad ‘every’ formulation and ignores the ordinary rule.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: A private organisation performs a public activity, but no governmental authority is shown to be involved in the alleged violation. Which position is most consistent with the general rule concerning writs?
o: A writ can never lie against a private organisation under any circumstances
A writ ordinarily lies because every public activity makes the organisation ‘State’
A writ does not ordinarily lie merely because the organisation performs a public activity
A writ lies only when Parliament specifically authorises the organisation
x: Writs do not ordinarily lie against private bodies merely on the basis of their public activity. The rule is not absolute, since State collusion can alter the position.
tq: Apply the ordinary rule while avoiding the absolute trap in the words ‘every’ and ‘never’.
sec: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

s: The demand to make the right to vote a Fundamental Right concerns a right which is presently regarded as:
o: A legal right derived exclusively from Article 21
A statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, with a constitutional basis under Article 326
A constitutional right enforceable only under Article 32
x: The right to vote is presently treated as statutory under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and is constitutionally connected with Article 326. It is not presently a Fundamental Right.
tq: Separate a statutory electoral right from a Fundamental Right and identify both cited provisions.
sec: Universal angles

s: The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that the rights to vote and contest elections are:
o: Natural rights outside the constitutional framework
Fundamental Rights available under Part III
x: The rights to vote and contest elections have been reaffirmed as statutory rights, rather than Fundamental Rights under Part III.
tq: Discriminate between the related but distinct rights to vote and contest and their legal status.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following groups of provisions is commonly described as the ‘golden triangle’ of the Constitution?
x: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are collectively described as the golden triangle because of their interrelationship in protecting liberty and individual rights.
tq: Recall the standard constitutional grouping rather than selecting adjacent Fundamental Rights articles.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
1. They operate as a check on governmental power.
2. They protect minorities.
3. They limit Parliament through Article 13.
4. They are regarded as a bulwark of liberty and the rule of law.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Fundamental Rights check governmental power, protect minorities, support liberty and the rule of law, and limit Parliament through Article 13.
tq: Test several connected constitutional purposes and choose the complete combination.
sec: Universal angles

s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the constitutional position in Britain from that in India regarding Fundamental Rights?
o: Britain has no codified Fundamental Rights; its rights rest on conventions and the rule of law
India, unlike Britain, protects rights only through conventions
Britain has a single written code of Fundamental Rights identical to Part III of India
Britain has no protection of rights because it follows neither conventions nor the rule of law
x: Britain does not have codified Fundamental Rights in the Indian constitutional sense; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.
tq: Compare the source and form of rights protection instead of confusing absence of codification with absence of rights.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Which of the following Articles and provisions were inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Article 31A
2. Article 31B
3. The Ninth Schedule
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The First Amendment Act, 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B and introduced the Ninth Schedule. The amendment is associated with the constitutional protection of certain land reform laws.
tq: Treat the amendment, its two Articles and the Schedule as one connected constitutional package.
sec: Universal angles

s: With reference to the Ninth Schedule, which statement is correct?
o: All laws placed in it are permanently immune from every form of judicial review
It contains only provisions relating to elections
Its protective effect has been subjected to limitations by the decision in I.R. Coelho (2007)
It was created by the Forty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1978
x: I.R. Coelho (2007) limited the absolute character of Ninth Schedule protection by permitting judicial scrutiny where basic-structure principles are affected.
tq: Use the later judicial limitation to reject the extreme claim of complete and permanent immunity.
sec: Universal angles

s:
Arrange the following developments in chronological order:
A. Decision in Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal
B. Decision in R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
C. Decision in Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib
D. Decision in Pradeep Kumar Biswas
x: The cases were decided in 1967, 1979, 1981 and 2002 respectively: Rajasthan SEB, R.D. Shetty, Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas.
tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the two closely related instrumentality decisions.
